arml-2019-power-01a.title: One switch per minute
arml-2019-power-01a.body:
Each switch must be flipped at least once and only one is flipped per minute, so at least 6 minutes are needed; flipping switches $1,2,\dots,6$ in turn works. $E(6,1)=6$.

**Answer: 6**

arml-2019-power-01b.title: Pairs
arml-2019-power-01b.body:
Every switch must be flipped, which needs at least $\frac62=3$ minutes; $\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\{5,6\}$ works. $E(6,2)=3$.

**Answer: 3**

arml-2019-power-01c.title: Lower bound and construction
arml-2019-power-01c.body:
In two minutes at most 6 switches can be flipped, so $E(7,3)\ge3$. The sets $\{1,2,3\},\{1,4,5\},\{1,6,7\}$ flip switch 1 three times and every other switch once, so all are on after 3 minutes. $E(7,3)=3$.

**Answer: 3**

arml-2019-power-01d.title: Parity rules out 2 minutes
arml-2019-power-01d.body:
One minute flips only 5 of 9 switches. In two minutes there are 10 flips; all 9 switches must be flipped at least once, so exactly one switch is flipped twice — and it ends up off. So $E(9,5)\ge3$. The sets $\{1,2,3,4,5\},\{1,2,3,6,7\},\{1,2,3,8,9\}$ flip $1,2,3$ three times and the rest once. $E(9,5)=3$.

**Answer: 3**

arml-2019-power-02a.title: Each switch once
arml-2019-power-02a.body:
At least $\frac n2$ minutes are needed to flip every switch once, and flipping $\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\dots,\{n-1,n\}$ achieves it. So $E(n,2)=\frac n2$.

**Answer: $E(n,2)=\frac n2$**

arml-2019-power-02b.title: Parity plus a construction
arml-2019-power-02b.body:
*Key fact (parity).* A switch is on exactly when it has been flipped an odd number of times. So after $m$ minutes with everything on, the total number of flips $mk$ is a sum of $n$ odd numbers: $mk\equiv n\pmod 2$.

Covering all $n=3a+2$ switches needs at least $a+1$ minutes. With exactly $a+1$ minutes there are $3a+3=n+1$ flips, which has the wrong parity. So $E(n,3)\ge a+2$.

Construction in $a+2$ minutes: $\{1,2,3\},\{1,2,4\},\{1,2,5\}$ (switches 1, 2 flipped three times, 3, 4, 5 once), then the remaining $3a-3$ switches $6,\dots,3a+2$ three at a time in $a-1$ minutes. Total $a+2$ minutes.

**Answer: $E(3a+2,3)=a+2$**

arml-2019-power-02c.title: Two minutes is not enough
arml-2019-power-02c.body:
One minute flips only $n-2<n$ switches. In two minutes each switch is flipped at most twice, so every switch would have to be flipped exactly once, needing $2(n-2)=n$, i.e. $n=4$. So for $n\ge5$, $E\ge3$.

Three minutes suffice: $\{1,4,5,\dots,n\}$, $\{2,4,5,\dots,n\}$, $\{3,4,5,\dots,n\}$ (each of size $n-2$) flip switches $1,2,3$ once and switches $4,\dots,n$ three times. So $E(n,n-2)=3$.

**Answer: 3**

arml-2019-power-03.title: Parity
arml-2019-power-03.body:
Take any even $k$ (e.g. $k=2$). Each flip changes the number of lit switches by $\pm1$, so a minute of $k$ flips changes it by an even amount. Starting from $0$, the number of lit switches is always even, so it can never be $2019$. Hence $E(2019,k)=\infty$ for every even $k$ with $2\le k\le2018$.

**Answer: e.g. $k=2$ (any even $k$)**

arml-2019-power-04a.title: Lower bound and explicit strategy
arml-2019-power-04a.body:
$E\ne1$ since $k<n$. In two minutes there are $2k>n$ flips, so some switch is flipped twice (and every switch at most twice), leaving it off; so $E\ne2$.

Since $n+k$ is even, so is $3k-n=(n+k)+2(k-n)$; write $3k-n=2b$. Then $b>0$ (as $3k>n$) and $b<k$ (as $k<n$). Also $n-b=3k-2b-b=3(k-b)$.

Each minute, flip switches $1,\dots,b$ together with a new block of $k-b$ of the remaining $3(k-b)$ switches. After 3 minutes, switches $1,\dots,b$ have been flipped 3 times and all others once — all on. So $E(n,k)=3$. ∎

arml-2019-power-04b.title: Complement each minute
arml-2019-power-04b.body:
*Key fact (parity).* A switch is on exactly when it has been flipped an odd number of times. So after $m$ minutes with everything on, the total number of flips $mk$ is a sum of $n$ odd numbers: $mk\equiv n\pmod 2$.

Here $n$ is even and $k$ is odd, so any escaping sequence has an even number $m$ of minutes. Note $n-k$ is also odd.

Take an escaping sequence of $m$ minutes for $(n,k)$ and replace each minute's set by its complement (size $n-k$). A switch flipped $f$ times originally (with $f$ odd) is now flipped $m-f$ times, which is odd since $m$ is even. So after $m$ minutes every switch is on, and $E(n,n-k)\le E(n,k)$. The same argument with $n-k$ in place of $k$ gives $E(n,k)\le E(n,n-k)$. (If one is $\infty$ so is the other.) Hence $E(n,k)=E(n,n-k)$. ∎

arml-2019-power-05a.title: Reduce to k = 27
arml-2019-power-05a.body:
$E(2020,1993)=E(2020,27)$. Since $27\cdot74=1998<2020$, at least 75 minutes are needed to flip every switch; and with $n$ even, $k$ odd the number of minutes must be even (total flips $27m\equiv2020\pmod2$), so at least $76$.

76 minutes suffice: for the first 33 minutes flip switch 1 together with 26 not-yet-flipped switches. Then switch 1 has been flipped 33 times (odd) and switches $2,\dots,859$ once, so $1,\dots,859$ are on. The remaining $2020-859=1161=27\cdot43$ switches are flipped once each in 43 more minutes. Total $33+43=76$.

**Answer: 76**

arml-2019-power-05b.title: Parity and a construction
arml-2019-power-05b.body:
Three minutes give only $1503<2001$ flips. Four minutes give $2004$ flips: covering all 2001 switches leaves 3 extra flips, so some switch gets an even number of flips (parity: $4\cdot501$ is even but a sum of 2001 odd numbers is odd). So $E\ge5$.

Five minutes: $5\cdot501=2505=2001+504$, so let 252 switches be flipped three times and the rest once. In each of minutes 1–3 flip switches $1,\dots,252$ plus 249 new switches; in minutes 4 and 5 flip 501 new switches each. New switches used: $3\cdot249+2\cdot501=1749=2001-252$ ✓. All switches end on, so $E(2001,501)=5$.

**Answer: 5**

arml-2019-power-06a.title: Reuse b switches three times
arml-2019-power-06a.body:
If $k\mid n$, flip disjoint blocks: $E=\frac nk$. Otherwise let $r=\lceil\frac nk\rceil$, so $(r-1)k<n<rk$; $r-1$ minutes cannot touch every switch, so $E\ge r$. Since $k\le\frac n2$ and $k\nmid n$, $r\ge3$.

$rk-n$ is even (both $n,k$ even); write $rk-n=2b$ with $1\le b$, and $b<k$ because $rk-n<k$.

- Minutes 1–3: flip switches $1,\dots,b$ plus $k-b$ switches never flipped before. Afterwards switches $1,\dots,b$ (flipped 3 times) and $3(k-b)$ others are on: $b+3(k-b)=3k-2b=n-k(r-3)$ switches.
- Minutes $4,\dots,r$: flip $k$ fresh switches each, covering the remaining $k(r-3)$.

All switches are on after $r$ minutes, so $E(n,k)=r=\lceil\frac nk\rceil$. ∎

arml-2019-power-06b.title: Two parity cases
arml-2019-power-06b.body:
If $k\mid n$, $E=\frac nk$. Otherwise let $r=\lceil\frac nk\rceil\ge3$, so $(r-1)k<n<rk$ and $E\ge r$. Since $k$ is odd, exactly one of $rk-n$ and $(r+1)k-n$ is even.

**Case 1: $rk-n=2b$.** As in the even case, $1\le b<k$. In minutes 1–3 flip switches $1,\dots,b$ plus $k-b$ fresh switches; this lights $3k-2b=n-k(r-3)$ switches. In the remaining $r-3$ minutes flip $k$ fresh switches each. Escape in $r$ minutes.

**Case 2: $(r+1)k-n=2b$.** Since $k<(r+1)k-n<2k$, we get $1\le b<k$. Minutes 1–3 as before light $3k-2b=n-k(r-2)$ switches, and $r-2$ further minutes of fresh switches finish. Escape in $r+1$ minutes.

So $r\le E(n,k)\le r+1$. ∎

arml-2019-power-07.title: Sort by parity and size
arml-2019-power-07.body:
*Key fact (parity).* A switch is on exactly when it has been flipped an odd number of times. So after $m$ minutes with everything on, the total number of flips $mk$ is a sum of $n$ odd numbers: $mk\equiv n\pmod 2$.

- $n$ odd, $k$ even: $E=\infty$ (an even number of flips per minute keeps the number of lit switches even).
- $n$ even, $k$ odd: the number of minutes must be even, so $E\ne3$.
- $k=n$: $E=1$. $k<\frac n3$: three minutes flip fewer than $n$ switches, so $E>3$.

Now let $n\equiv k\pmod2$ and $\frac n3\le k<n$.
- $\frac n2<k<n$: $E=3$ (shown by flipping switches $1,\dots,b$ three times, where $3k-n=2b$, and the rest once).
- $k=\frac n2$: $E=2$ (two disjoint halves).
- $\frac n3\le k<\frac n2$: then $\lceil\frac nk\rceil=3$. If $k=\frac n3$, $E=3$ by three disjoint blocks. Otherwise $3k-n$ is even and positive, $3k-n=2b$ with $b<k$; flipping switches $1,\dots,b$ every minute plus $k-b$ fresh ones lights all $3k-2b=n$ switches in 3 minutes, and 2 minutes cannot cover $n>2k$ switches. So $E=3$.

Hence $E(n,k)=3$ iff $n+k$ is even, $\frac n3\le k<n$ and $k\ne\frac n2$.

*(The official solution states the condition as "$n+k$ even and $\frac n3\le k<n$", overlooking $k=\frac n2$, e.g. $E(4,2)=2$.)*

arml-2019-power-08b.title: E(5,3) = 3
arml-2019-power-08b.body:
$5=3\cdot1+2$, so $E(5,3)=1+2=3$ (two minutes give 6 flips, wrong parity for 5 switches; three minutes: $\{1,2,3\},\{1,2,4\},\{1,2,5\}$). Then $I(5,3)=3-\frac53=\frac43$.

**Answer: $\frac{4}{3}$**

arml-2019-power-08c.title: Aim for E = 3
arml-2019-power-08c.body:
Try $E(n,k)=3$: then $\frac nk=3-\frac{15}8=\frac98$. Take $n=18$, $k=16$: same parity and $\frac n2<k<n$, so $E(18,16)=3$ (with $3k-n=30=2\cdot15$: flip switches $1,\dots,15$ every minute plus one new switch each minute). Then $I(18,16)=3-\frac{18}{16}=\frac{15}8$.

**Answer: e.g. $(18,16)$**

arml-2019-power-08d.title: Use the complement symmetry
arml-2019-power-08d.body:
Let $n=2x$, $k=2x-1$. Since $n$ is even and $k$ odd, $E(n,k)=E(n,n-k)=E(2x,1)=2x$ (complementing each minute's set preserves solutions, as the number of minutes is even). So
$$I(n,k)=2x-\frac{2x}{2x-1}.$$
For $x>2$, $\frac{2x}{2x-1}<2<x$, hence $I(n,k)>2x-x=x$. ∎

arml-2019-power-09.title: Bound and approach
arml-2019-power-09.body:
**Upper bound.** For $k<\frac n2$ with $I$ defined, $E(n,k)\le\lceil\frac nk\rceil+1$ (for $k$ even $n$ must be even, and $E=\lceil\frac nk\rceil$). Since $\lceil y\rceil-y<1$, $I(n,k)\le\lceil\frac nk\rceil+1-\frac nk<2$.

**Approaching 2.** Let $k\ge3$ be odd and $n=3k+2$ (odd). Then $\lceil\frac nk\rceil=4$. The number of minutes must be odd (total flips $mk\equiv n\pmod2$ with $k,n$ odd), so $E\ne4$, hence $E=5$. Thus
$$I(3k+2,k)=5-\frac{3k+2}k=2-\frac2k,$$
which is arbitrarily close to 2 for large odd $k$.

So the least upper bound of $S$ is $2$ (not attained).

**Answer: 2**

arml-2019-power-10.title: Where can large inefficiencies come from?
arml-2019-power-10.body:
**Step 1: $I(n,k)>2$ forces $n$ even, $k$ odd, $\frac n2<k<n$.**
- $k=n$: $I=0$.
- $k\le\frac n2$: by the results on $E$ for $k\le\frac n2$ ($E=\lceil\frac nk\rceil$ for $n,k$ even; $E\le\lceil\frac nk\rceil+1$ for $k$ odd; undefined for $k$ even, $n$ odd), $I\le\lceil\frac nk\rceil+1-\frac nk<2$.
- $\frac n2<k<n$ and $n+k$ even: $E=3$, so $I=3-\frac nk<2$.
- $n$ odd, $k$ even: undefined.

**Step 2: $q_1=\frac{11}3$.** If $I(n,k)=\frac{11}3$, then by Step 1 $1<\frac nk<2$, and $E=\frac{11}3+\frac nk$ is an integer in $(\frac{14}3,\frac{17}3)$, so $E=5$ and $\frac nk=\frac43$: $n=4m$, $k=3m$ with $m$ odd. By the complement symmetry $E(4m,3m)=E(4m,m)$, and $m\mid4m$ gives $E(4m,m)\le4$ (four disjoint blocks). So $E\le4\ne5$. Contradiction.

**Step 3: $q_2=\frac{17}5$.** Similarly $E\in(\frac{22}5,\frac{27}5)$ forces $E=5$ and $\frac nk=\frac85$: $n=8m$, $k=5m$, $m$ odd. Then $E(8m,5m)=E(8m,3m)$; with $k'=3m$ odd and $k'\le\frac n2$, $E\le\lceil\frac83\rceil+1=4$. Again $E\ne5$.

So neither $\frac{11}3$ nor $\frac{17}5$ is an inefficiency. ∎ (A computer search over $n\le300$ agrees; $\frac52$ is another example.)
